I can't stress enough that when transporting fish you need a minimum of 50:50 ration of water to oxygen.

I work at a LFS one day a week. For the past 4 weeks there was this beautiful blue trigger kept in the Marine tanks. It went to a good home in a large tank and everything, however it was spitting water out of the tank and chasing the other smaller fish, so today it was brought back.

Unfortunately, there had been an accident on the roads and it was left in the bag too long with not enough oxygen for the size of the fish. In the stifling heat as well. When it came in, the owner (Pete) emptied the fish into a bucket and told me to get some salt water from the back quickly as he acclimatised the fish to the water of the tank it would go into. The poor fish was on its side gasping for air. He left it when another customer came in with more fish.

She'd come in earlier to ask if it was okay to drop her gold fish and pleco off and he gave her the bags. They lived round the corner to the shop but all three goldfish were huge and on the turn by the time they got here. She brought the bags in a bucket. She'd have been better just carrying the fish in the bucket than in the bags. Luckily they weren't in as bad a way as the trigger is. But they were in too much water.

The trigger however, may not see through the night. He had enough energy to splash the hell out of Pete as he put it in the tank, but I really hope that poor fish makes it through.

When it comes to transporting large fish, large plastic containers are the best and you need to make sure they have more air than water. Because big fish use more air than little fish. So please, if you need to transport fish remember that 50:50 air to water unless they're a big fish, then you're looking at 75:25 air to water. Just enough to cover their body will do for them to swim in. Don't worry too much about that, it can recover more from a trip with less water than a trip with less oxygen. If you can, add some oxygenation tablets to the water to give it that boost if your unsure on traffic situations.

This is why I don't like keeping fish sometimes, because while I know that it's a bit of a hard one to get into, there's just so many stupid people out there throwing out garbage advice, if at all! And you just know that there are plenty of folks who have that "oh well it's just a fish it'll be fine!!!" mentality.

I personally don't like bags for transporting, but it'll never stop. All I can hope for is that people know how to do it. Me and my husband went to our LFS to get a fancy male guppy to put in a 10 that has female feeders in it. The kid who got our guppy was (softly) bouncing this fish on the counter and rolling it around. I was so close to telling him that that's a live animal in that bag, and should probably stop. I was pretty pissed even after we left.

When I was getting my Oranda and Dojo loach back from my husbands parents in CA (long story short, we moved between three states in two years T-T), his dad brought them both up in one of those 25lbs tubs that kitty litter comes in. We had rigged it with a battery-powered air pump, though, because we planned on taking them with us in the first place, but didn't have any more room. So they came up from Southern CA to ND, a two day drive getting sloshed and bonked around, and they arrived just fine! Stressed out, but fine, they are now living it up in a 60gal. :) But other than that, I use the same bucket for everything fish-related, buckets are great!

I feel so bad for that fish in question though, that's really unfortunate. I hope the guy makes it through! This isn't really a subject I've seen brought up a whole lot either, so a nice change! I've always and will always suggest buckets for transporting any fish, it's just far easier and safer in the long run!
